en: It is stated that those who seek unsurpassed bodhi must surely maintain the prohibitions and precepts with diligence. Once the precepts are maintained with purity, meditative concentration and wisdom will naturally manifest before one.
Therefore, to maintain the precepts with purity, one must not depart from the ordinary course of daily life; in every action of the day, one must never forget the precepts.

Because it is naturally pure and luminous, one must—whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, eating, dressing, or even during the acts of defecating and urinating—be careful never to neglect it for even a moment. Thus, the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"If Bodhisattvas skillfully employ their minds, they will obtain all supreme and wondrous merits from the Buddhas."

The Dharma-mind is without obstruction. It is further said that when a Bodhisattva employs the mind in this way, none among all the world’s devas, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, gandharvas, asuras, and even all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas can shake it.
Judging from this, one who diligently cultivates the precepts and maintains sublime conduct is truly not a minor being.
How could one dare to neglect or fail to study that which is compared to a vehicle?
Therefore, a bhikṣu who upholds the precepts should rely on each and every practice within the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" (Śīla-varga), so as not to betray his resolve for renunciation.

However, because many beginners are dull-witted and unable to carry out the practices in their entirety, there is no choice but to take the broad and extract the concise, and furthermore, to [rely upon this].
I have compiled the mantras of the Ancient Guhyasamāja tradition and appended them for the convenience of beginners, titling this work *The Daily Use of the Vinaya*.
May practitioners apply these forms during the six periods of the day and night to clarify their own minds as the cause of unsurpassed bodhi;
through this, may they enter [the path]. Desiring that it be widely disseminated, I have respectfully composed this preface. Written by the practitioner Xingzhi.

*The Daily Practice of the Vinaya (Vinaya Riju-yong Lu)*. Regarding the "Daily Practice of the Vinaya," there has long existed a record of the characteristics of the precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*) that has been circulated. Although its textual content is complete, it lacks proper order;
thus, those who receive and uphold it seem not to have grasped its systematic arrangement. What is recorded here follows [the tradition of] Xuancheng...
The *Kuhai funyō* (Life-raft in the Sea of Suffering) compiled by Master Kuei is for the most part identical [to this work], though there are slight differences in its supplementary sections.
Scholars should value the merit of reciting it; take care not to harbor mutual doubts or criticisms.
Whenever the practitioner awakens from sleep, they should immediately recite these words softly and silently:
"Sleep has now awakened; I vow that all sentient beings May awaken with all-encompassing wisdom And look upon the ten directions.
Oṃ dhīra dhīra svāhā. (Recite seven times.)
Whenever one hears the sound of a bell, whether struck by another or by oneself, one should recite:
"May this sound of the bell transcend the Dharma-realm; May it be heard throughout the dark depths of the Iron Ring Mountains.
Through hearing, may the dust of the senses be purified and perfect penetration realized; May all sentient beings attain true enlightenment."
Hearing the sound of the bell, afflictions grow light; wisdom increases, and Bodhi arises.
Leaving hell behind, emerging from the fiery pit, may one attain Buddhahood and deliver all sentient beings.
The Mantra for Destroying Hell states:
Oṃ karateye svāhā (seven times).
Furthermore, when the practitioner is sleeping, upon hearing the sound of the bell, they should immediately rise and sit;
they must be careful not to succumb to indolence or laziness, lest they bring calamity and misfortune upon themselves.
An ancient worthy said:
"If one hears the bell and lies down without rising, The guardian deity of the bed will be incensed. In this life there will be no fortune or wisdom;
After death, one will fall into the body of a snake. Those who are ill should remain seated; For those whose illness is grave, this does not apply."
When the practitioner dons his robes at dawn upon descending from the platform, he recites this verse:
"When donning the upper robe, I vow that all sentient beings shall attain supreme roots of goodness and reach the further shore of the Dharma.
When donning the lower skirt, I vow that all sentient beings shall clothe themselves in all roots of goodness and be fully endowed with shame and remorse."
Adjusting one’s robes and fastening the belt, one should wish that all sentient beings restrain their roots of goodness so they are not lost or scattered.
(At this point, when lowering oneself onto the seat, one should snap the fingers three times.
When setting down one’s feet and remaining seated, one should wish that all sentient beings attain liberation of mind and dwell in immovable stability.
From the dawn of the morning until the evening, may all sentient beings protect themselves;
if anyone should lose their life beneath your feet, may they be reborn immediately in the Pure Land.
Oṃ yidhi lūni svāhā. (Recite seven times.)
When walking, do not harm insects; the verse and mantra say:
When lifting the foot, one should wish that all sentient beings may emerge from the sea of birth and death and be endowed with all wholesome dharmas.
Oṃ dhiḥ liri liri svāhā. (Recite seven times.)

Regarding the ritual for using the toilet, the *Jizumen Jingxun* (Admonitions for the Gate of the Black Robes) states: "The laws and regulations governing the use of the toilet are meticulously detailed because one wishes to purify and solemnize the vessel of the body in order to draw near to the sages and worthies.
There are specific protocols for both cleansing and washing the hands; if these are not fully understood, one will instead defile one's own hands."

In performing rituals, reciting sutras, burning incense, or joining one's palms, even the slightest movement may lead to fault; how can one not be cautious? I shall now slightly revise and expand upon ancient regulations.
However, as for minute details of conduct, it is truly difficult to enumerate them all. Generally, at every moment of activity, there are skillful means;
regarding the protection of the human sense-faculties, one should naturally extend these principles by analogy. Does not the Book say: "The way of Heaven is like water"? (Analects 15.6)

If one does not heed minor details of conduct, they will eventually bring ruin to one’s great virtue; how much more so for those in the monastic order! I hope that those of high intelligence will encourage their juniors accordingly.

As the Sūtra says: "If one enters the latrine without washing clean after defecating, one shall not be admitted among the ranks of the Great Sangha, nor may one sit upon the meditation platform, nor ascend the precious hall," and so forth.
When first entering the latrine, one must first snap the fingers three times to alert those within.
Knowing that one must not force the attendants to come out, one should further snap the fingers three times to alert the ghosts dwelling in impurity,
silently reciting the mantra: Oṃ hulu-dhaye svāhā (seven times).

Furthermore, one must not spit phlegm into the latrine to harm the spirits dwelling in filth; these two points of hidden virtue (*guṇa*) are fully recorded in the Tripiṭaka, so they are not cited here at length.
When first squatting, one must first pour a small amount of water into the basin:
first, to dissolve the odor of old excrement; second, so that new excrement passes easily without accumulating in the basin. Then, one should reflect as follows:
When defecating or urinating, one should make this aspiration: "May all sentient beings abandon greed, hatred, and delusion, and eliminate all unwholesome dharmas.
Oṃ śrīye bhaḥ svāhā. (Recite seven times.
Furthermore, one must not strain the breath or make noise; one must not lower the head to look down; one must not spit against the wall or converse with others.
The details are exactly as described in the Vinaya, so I shall not cite them at length here. Upon finishing the washing, the verse says:
"When the task is finished, approach the water; I vow that all sentient beings shall swiftly proceed within the supramundane Dharma.
It further states:
Washing away physical impurities, may all sentient beings be pure, harmonious, and supple, ultimately free from defilement.
Oṃ ha na mi li te svāhā. (Recite seven times.
The aforementioned three mantras each have different placements; however, one may practice and uphold any single dharma among them.
To obtain supreme benefit:
recite this verse and mantra while washing the palms with water. One should then make this aspiration: May all sentient beings obtain pure hands And receive, uphold, and maintain the Buddha-dharma.
Oṃ Jukāraya Svāhā (recite seven times, or up to twenty-one times for greater efficacy).
When washing the hands, one should use these three substances—ash, clay, and soap-nut—or soap-bean pods, washing each with seven applications in succession;
the back of the hand should be treated in the same way. If the number of applications is reduced, one must certainly use both clay and soap; these two must not be omitted. As it says:
Alternatively, it may not be so, for in the end it results in impurity. Thus, the *Jingxun of the Black Gate* states:
"During the Yuanyou era, there was a monk from Shu named Dharma Master Zhichao who had been constantly reciting the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* for thirty years.

One day he happened to see a youth of refined appearance who raised his hand in a high bow. The Master asked, 'Where have you come from? The youth replied, 'From Mount Wutai. The Master [further] asked...
He asked, "Why have you come from so far away? The other replied, "I have a small matter for which I wish to guide you. Hui-chao said, "I would like to hear it.
The other said, "It is certainly praiseworthy that your teacher recites the sutras;

however, his error lies in the fact that when he washes himself after using the toilet, he touches water and lets it drip onto the back of his hand without ever using ash or mud to cleanse it. According to the Vinaya regulations, ash and mud must be used."
"Seven times previously, you had only two or three conditions for this contact to remain; now, even your prostrating to the Buddha and reciting the sutras all result in offense.
Having spoken these words, he vanished. Chao felt ashamed and reformed his ways. Those who understood said, "This must have been a manifestation by Mañjuśrī to provide a warning to Chao.
Thus one knows that washing the hands must be performed according to the Dharma, as stated in the *Karmaprajñapti-sūtra*.
It is said that by touching [the ground] with one's hand while requesting the sutra, one shall receive the retribution of becoming a worm in a latrine;

furthermore, there are many other matters of ritual protocol clearly explained as warnings and instructions, which must be known from within the Vinaya section. (In the sutras, there are specific divine mantras for entering the latrine and for cleansing;
if one does not silently recite these mantras, even if one washes with the waters of seven Ganges Rivers, the body and its vessels will not become pure. Why is this? Because the seeds are impure.)
Mantra for Washing the Face with Water:
When washing the face with water, one should make this aspiration: "May all sentient beings attain the gateway to the pure Dharma, and be forever free from defilement.
Oṃ raṃ (twenty-one times) svāhā.
A Verse for Chanting Over Drinking Water:
The Buddha Contemplates a Single Bowl of Water. Within it dwell eighty-four thousand insects; If one does not recite this mantra, it is as if eating the flesh of sentient beings.
Oṃ vaśiparamaṇi svāhā (recite seven times; it is even more excellent to drink water after first prostrating to the Buddha as before).

Donning the robes and spreading out the sitting mat, recite this verse and mantra while putting on the *kāṣāya* robe: May all sentient beings have minds unstained by defilement, And fully realize the Way of the Great Sage.
The five robes are said to be "excellent garments of liberation," the signless field of merit robe; I now receive them upon my head,
never to be parted from them throughout all lifetimes.
Oṃ siddhaye svāhā (seven times). Seven Robes:
"Excellent is this garment of liberation, the signless field of merit robe; I now receive it upon my head."
May I always, in every lifetime, obtain [this robe].
Oṃ dhupe dhupe svāhā (seven times). Thus says the Mahāsaṃghika Vinaya.
When donning the saṃghāṭī, one should wish that all sentient beings enter the foremost stage and attain the dharma of immovability.
How excellent is this robe of liberation, this signless field of merit! Now, wearing it upon my head, may I widely deliver all deluded multitudes.
Oṃ mahākāpapataye svāhā (seven times). Whether arriving before the Buddha or entering the *maṇḍala*, before spreading out the ritual implements, first recite this verse and mantra:
If one should behold the Buddha, May all sentient beings thereby Attain the unimpeded eye And see all Buddhas.
Oṃ amṛte hūṃ phaṭ (seven times). Spreading the bedding:
*niṣīdana*. Nourishing the sprout of the mind-nature, one unfolds and ascends to the ground of the sages.
To carry out the Tathāgata’s command,
recite: *Oṃ damba damba svāhā* (seven times),
or chant the verse of praise to the Buddha:

Dharma King, Unsurpassed Honored One, peerless throughout the three realms, Teacher of gods and humans, compassionate father of the four modes of birth— I now take refuge in you; swiftly extinguish the karma of three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
To extol and praise you would not reach its end even in a hundred million *kalpas*.
The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī prostrated before the Buddha and spoke this verse of contemplation and incantation:
"The nature of the one who prostrates and the object of prostration is empty and quiescent; the resonance and response of the Way are inconceivable.
This place of my practice is like the jewel of Indra, within which the reflections of all Buddhas of the ten directions appear. (The two characters for "Buddhas" are repeated.)
Alternatively, Bodhisattvas, Arhats, and others may modify it as appropriate: "My own body and shadow appear before all Buddhas" (the Buddhas also modify it according to their will).
With head bowed to touch their feet, I take refuge and pay homage:

Oṃ vajra hūṃ. (Recite seven times; "hūṃ" is pronounced with a secret tone. Some say it is "vajra muḥ," also pronounced with a secret tone. Others say it is "vajra hoḥ. These Sanskrit sounds differ in their dialectal variations; recite whichever one you maintain.)
The Dharma is the very nature of reality, empty and like space; This eternally abiding Dharma-treasure is inconceivable.
My own reflection appears before this Dharma-treasure; With single-minded devotion, I take refuge and pay homage according to the Dharma.

(This is the verse for prostration; the mantra is the same as above, recited seven times. Alternatively, one may perform prostrations with the Three Refuges at any convenient time (it is even better to include the preceding verse and mantra).
When prostrating before a stūpa, the verse for circumambulation says:
"I prostrate before the stūpa; may all sentient beings have no one among gods or humans able to see the crown of their heads.
When circumambulating the stūpa three times: "May all sentient beings diligently seek the Buddha-way, their minds never wearying or ceasing."
Namo samanta-buddhānām oṃ dhupe dhupe svāhā (seven times).
Having performed prostrations and praises, one should thereafter recite [the mantra] while making individual vows for rebirth in the Western Paradise.
A bhikṣu must not wear the *kaṣāya* over both shoulders when paying homage to Buddha-stūpas, temples, and the like.

If one dies and falls into the Iron Armor Hell, one must therefore exclude those who are sitting in meditation, receiving food, or wearing the robe over both shoulders (wearing it over both shoulders means draping it across both shoulders);

these do not constitute an offense. Furthermore, a bhikṣu must not wear his meditation robe while prostrating before the Buddha, even toward his elders, nor while walking in circumambulation before a Buddha’s stūpa or temple;
otherwise, upon death, he will fall among the species of tortoises, turtles, soft-shelled turtles, and crocodiles. Therefore, be careful, be careful!
Holding the *khakkhara* (staff), he recited the verse:
"Holding this *khakkhara* staff, I vow that all sentient beings shall establish great assemblies of giving and demonstrate the path of reality."
Oṃ kṛṇa kṛṇa kṛnta patti naṭi naye bhaṇi hūṃ phaṭ (seven times).
The verse for begging alms says:
Entering the village to beg for food, one should wish that all sentient beings enter the profound Dharma-realm with minds free from obstruction.
Oṃ chile jule cundī svāhā (seven times). At the time of eating, the verse and mantra for spreading out the bowl are as follows:
The Tathāgata is the vessel of measure; now I am able to spread forth [offerings].
May I offer to all the assemblies, with the three spheres empty and quiescent. Oṃ smara maṇi svāhā. (Recite seven times.)
The Verse on the Empty Bowl and the Full Bowl says:
If one sees an empty bowl, one should wish that all sentient beings have minds so pure they are empty of afflictions.
If one sees a full bowl, one should wish that all sentient beings be fully endowed with and perfected in all wholesome dharmas.
Oṃ bhrūṃ (seven times). When receiving food, whether sitting in the full lotus posture or in any suitable position, spread a cloth over one's knees;
hold the bowl with the left hand and support its rim with the right, while reciting the offering according to the standard ritual procedure as previously explained.
Having completed these reflections, one should recite the *Lam* mantra twenty-one times according to the ritual for making offerings to the Buddhas and benefiting sentient beings;
then, further recite the mantra for transforming food twenty-one times. Thereafter, recite the verse for generating [the feast] and the dharani as follows:
The power of the Dharma is inconceivable; Great compassion is without obstruction. Seven grains pervade the ten directions, Universally bestowed throughout the entire realm of dust.
Oṃ ture svāhā. (Recite seven times; this is for use at the morning meal.)
Great Garuḍa Golden-Winged Bird, The hosts of spirits in the vast wilderness, Rākṣasas, and the Mother of Ghost Children— May they all be filled with nectar!

Oṃ mudite svāhā. (Recite seven times; this is used for the midday meal offering. However, although there appear to be differences between what is recited at the two sessions, they may also be unified as the verse says:)
The power of the Dharma is inconceivable; compassion is without obstruction. Seven grains pervade the ten directions, universally bestowed throughout the entire realm of sand.

May the Mother of Ghosts, the Deity of the Wilderness, and the King of the Golden-Winged Birds all be fully satiated. (The mantra is as above. For the attendant who delivers the food, the verse and mantra for the offering are as follows:)
"You hosts of spirits and deities, I now bestow this offering upon you. May this food pervade the ten directions for all spirits and deities to consume together.

Oṃ muḥ liṅ svāhā" (Recite seven times). If there is no attendant, one may deliver it oneself in the same manner. After the rite of generation, one should interlace the ten fingers of both hands with the palms facing outward, pressing the right hand over the left to form the seal.
Seal the crown of the head and recite the mantra of the syllable *Oṃ* twenty-one times; then further recite *Oṃ Vajra Hūṃ* seven times—this is even more sublime.

If a practitioner can perform each of these rites exactly as described above, then by the power of the empowerment of these divine mantras, they will be able to offer the seven treasures, a hundred flavors, and various foods, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, to the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and all the Arhats and noble Saṅgha, pervading everywhere. Their merit and virtue are truly inconceivable.

Yet, those practitioners today are unable to follow the teachings themselves, and when they see others practicing them, they instead treat them with contempt and ridicule. How bitter this is! It is truly a great pity. Thereafter, hold up the bowl and chant the mantra, saying: (Here follows the mantra.)
Holding the alms-bowl, one should wish that all sentient beings may become vessels of the Dharma and receive the offerings of devas and humans.
Oṃ kili kili vajra hūṃ phaṭ (recite seven times). While formally receiving the food, one should maintain the five reflections and use three scoops of the bowl.
First, reflect on the labor expended: measure the distance from where the food came; for this single bowl of rice, the laborer’s sweat flowed.

Second, one should reflect upon one’s own virtues and conduct to determine whether one is fully qualified or deficient for receiving offerings. If one is deficient, it is inappropriate; if fully qualified, one may accept them.
Third, guarding the mind to remain free from faults takes the abandonment of greed and the like as its principle. One must distance oneself from these three faults—greed, hatred, and delusion.
Fourth, wholesome food is the medicine for treating the withered body, for the sake of curing the ailments of hunger and thirst; thus, food must be regarded as medicine.
Fifth, for the sake of attaining the Way, one should accept this food; if one does not eat, illness will arise—whence could the work of the Way proceed?
First vow: to sever all evil completely. Second vow: to cultivate all good until it is fulfilled. Third vow: to deliver all sentient beings.
Some say that dedicating the fruits of the three types of cultivated goodness to sentient beings—meaning that all may together attain Buddhahood—is also permissible.

When a practitioner receives food at the two prescribed times, they must necessarily form the mental visualization of these five contemplations; furthermore, they should visualize the food as putrid, festering, and impure, and only then take the three spoonfuls with the vow to eat. An ancient saying goes: "Do not violate the five contemplations; observe moderation in the three spoonfuls. Even if one were to first take the three spoonfuls and subsequently perform the five contemplations, it would still be acceptable.

Sengba said: "The Buddha established the rule that bhikṣus maintain the five contemplations while eating. How difficult it is to digest the offerings of the faithful if the mind is distracted by idle chatter! Having heard these words, how can one not be cautious? One should first recite this before concluding the meal."
The verse following the Cundī Dhāraṇī says:
"Those who practice giving will surely obtain its benefit; if one gives for the sake of happiness, one will subsequently attain peace and joy."
When the meal is finished, one should wish that all sentient beings accomplish all that they have to do and be fully endowed with all Buddha-dharmas.
The verse for receiving the offering says:
"The two gifts of wealth and Dharma are equal and without distinction; may the *dānapāramitā* be fully perfected."
The verse and incantation for washing the alms bowl says:
"By means of this water used to wash the bowl, which possesses a flavor like celestial nectar, I bestow it upon all the spirits and ghosts,
causing them all to obtain full satisfaction."

Oṃ maheśvara svāhā (recite seven times). First, rinse [the object] with pure water; this water may be disposed of on clean ground, in a natural pond, or in a clean river or flowing stream—it will bring benefit in all such places.
By no means discard it in a defiled place. Afterwards, wash the inside and outside with pure water, then wipe it dry with a clean cloth. Once it is dry, it is ready for use.
The verse and mantra for chewing the *dantakāṣṭha* (tooth-stick) say:
Holding the tooth-stick in hand, I vow that all sentient beings May attain the wondrous Dharma And reach ultimate purity.
While chewing the tooth-stick, I vow that all sentient beings May have minds that are harmonious and pure, Consuming all afflictions.
Oṃ laṃ oṃ laṃ (twenty-one times) svāhā. (Laṃ is the old reading for raṃ.
Furthermore, the mantra says:
Oṃ amogha-male-īvara-kara-saṃsthite padma-kumāre īvara-saṃsthe dhara dhara sumi maṇḍe svāhā.
(Recite seven times; if it is too cumbersome, one may simply recite the preceding Oṃ-raṃ mantra. There are five benefits to chewing the tooth-stick: first, the mouth will not be bitter;

second, the mouth will not be foul-smelling; third, wind disorders are removed; fourth, heat disorders are removed; fifth, phlegm is removed. If one does not chew it, there are five faults: first, the mouth becomes bitter.

1. One must not distinguish between the odors of exhalations; 2. one must not distinguish between tastes; 3. phlegm must not remain undissolved; 4. one must not suppress the urge for food; 5. the eyes must not be blurred. When chewing, one must stay in a secluded place and not face a Buddhist stūpa, nor any other clean areas where people come and go.

When discarding the tooth-stick, first rinse it with water, then snap one's fingers in a secluded spot to alert others before casting it away. If taking a willow branch, one should ask permission from its guardian deity; if there is no guardian, one should greet the tree spirit before breaking it off. This instruction should also be applied to others.
One must not take branches from the center or the sides; only those [from the ends] are permissible. If one acts contrary to these instructions, one incurs an offense against the Dharma.
The Verse and Mantra for Shaving the Head:
Shaving off beard and hair, I vow that all sentient beings May distance themselves from afflictions And ultimately attain quiescent extinction.
Oṃ siddhantu mantradharāḥ svāhā. (Recite seven times. When shaving the head, one should follow the auspicious days selected by Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva.

It should be used on the fourth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, tenth, eleventh, fourteenth, fifteenth, sixteenth, nineteenth, twenty-second, twenty-third, twenty-fourth, twenty-fifth, twenty-sixth, twenty-ninth,
and thirtieth days of each month (as recorded in the Ratnakūṭa section).
Regarding the ritual for entering the bathhouse: whenever a bhikṣu enters the bathhouse, he should wear his five-strip robe (*pañcakaṭhina*).
If the location is inconvenient, he may instead wear whatever is appropriate. He should hang his clean robes on a clean pole and hang his soiled robes [on another].
On the staff for touching [the water], one should remove and put on clothes with composure and ease. Before bathing, one must first wash and rinse the feet;
this must be done with meticulous care so as not to touch the water before entering the bath-vessel. The verse and incantation for washing the feet and bathing is as follows:
When washing the feet, one should wish that all sentient beings be endowed with the power of the divine feet (*ṛddhipāda*), so that their actions are unimpeded.
When bathing the body, one should wish that all sentient beings be free from defilement in body and mind, radiant and pure within and without.

Oṃ vajra-naukhaṭa svāhā. (Recite seven times. One must not bathe in a public bathhouse, nor urinate there, nor speak or laugh with others. The *Human and Celestial Jewel Mirror* states: There was once a monk... [text fragment] ...who had a bowl.

While playing and laughing during a bath, he was reborn in the Hell of Boiling Water; how painful! How could one not be cautious that such a minor transgression might bring about such a great calamity?
When spreading out a mat or bedding for sitting meditation, the verse and mantra say:
"When spreading out a bed or seat, I vow that all sentient beings shall cause the wholesome dharmas to blossom and perceive the true reality."
Sitting upright with body straight, one should wish that all sentient beings sit upon the seat of Bodhi, their minds free from attachment.
Oṃ vatra ani-praṇidhaye svāhā. (Recite seven times. When a practitioner sits upright in meditation, they must be courageous and diligent, skillfully warding off dullness and distraction;

they should be careful not to be indolent, lazy, or heedless, nor allow themselves to succumb to torpor so as to cause the loss of wholesome dharmas. Therefore, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* says: "During the first and last watches of the night, do not let there be any neglect; during the middle watch, recite the sūtras."

Reflect upon this: do not let your life pass in vain and achieve nothing because of the causes and conditions of sleep. You must contemplate impermanence—the fire that consumes all worlds—and seek early deliverance for yourself; do not sleep! Contemplate this.
The verse for emerging from meditative absorption says:
"Leaving the cross-legged posture, I vow that all sentient beings shall contemplate all conditioned phenomena as ultimately returning to dispersal and extinction.
When about to fall asleep, one should join the palms, visualize the Buddha, and recite the following verse ten times:
When the mind rests in sleep, one should wish that all sentient beings may attain physical tranquility and that their minds be free from agitation.

(Furthermore, one should visualize this wheel of the syllable *A* and recite it twenty-one times with a single breath while lying on the right side. The above verse and mantra constitute the daily practice for one cycle. Thus, one should end and then begin again, beginning and then ending again;

one must strive to maintain this with constant diligence and without interruption. When this becomes long-practiced and matured until body and mind are purified, the merit of one's precepts and conduct will be spontaneously accomplished without seeking its fulfillment. Some may ask: "One..."

If one contemplates dependent origination as non-arising and transcends the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles, what is the use of daily recitation? It is said: "If one can truly do so, all such talk is superfluous. However, if this is not yet the case, you must diligently follow this practice and conduct.

Be careful not to claim attainment of what has not been attained, lest you become part of those who harbor the pride of overestimation (*adhimāna*). Cherish these daily verses and mantras. Beyond these, there are various names and forms recorded below for the convenience of beginners in their practice and upholding.
The characteristics of the five precepts for lay *upāsakas* and others are:
first, not killing; second, not stealing; third, not engaging in sexual misconduct;
fourth, not speaking falsehoods; fifth, not drinking alcohol or eating meat (as the consumption of meat was not included under the category of killing in ancient times).
The ten precepts for a renunciant śrāmaṇera are as follows:
first, not to kill; second, not to steal;
third, not to engage in sexual misconduct (that is, not to violate the practice of brahmacarya); fourth, not to speak falsely.
Fifth: not drinking alcohol or eating meat (as eating meat is also subsumed under the precept against killing, it is added here for the sake of beginners);
Sixth: not wearing flower garlands, jeweled necklaces, or applying fragrant oils to the body;

The *Jiànzi Mùlùn* (鍵鎡母論) translates this as the *Qiǎntiěbō Jīng* (淺鐵鉢經). The *Yīnshūsū* (音疏) states that the small bowl within a larger bowl is now called a *mèizi* (鐼子).
The *Shísòng Lǜ* (十誦律) refers to it as the "half-large *jiànzi*" (鍵鎡) or "small *jiànzi*" (小鍵鎡). The *Sìfēn Lǜ* (四分律) states that the *jiànzi* (鍵鎡) is inserted [into the larger bowl].
The small bowls enter into the medium bowls, and the medium bowls enter into the large bowl; furthermore, there is the *kujara*, which is translated here as "vessel according to the bowl.
The *Fǎbǎo* (Dharma Jewel) commentary explains that these refer to spoons, chopsticks, ladles (*jiānzī*), and so forth (*jiānzī* is pronounced qiánzī; the second character is read míngpíng).
In Sanskrit, *kuṇḍikā* means "vase" (*ping*) in Chinese; it is also called a *kuṇḍika*, which refers to a ritual washing vessel.

It is always kept filled with water and carried on one's person for the purpose of purifying the hands. The *Jigui zhuan* (Record of Things Sent Back from the West) states that there are two types of *kuṇḍikā*:
those made of ceramic or earthenware are for pure use, while those made of copper or iron are for contact use. (The following explains the water filter.)
*Parissāvana* (translated here as "water-strainer")—the *Zhengji* (Correct Record) states:
"In the West, white woolen cloth is used; in the land of the East (China), fine silk is appropriate. If raw silk allows small insects to pass through directly, one should use boiled silk for it.
The *Zenghui ji* (Record of Augmented Radiance) states: "Though its form appears light and small, when examining its function, it serves to protect living beings; this is precisely compassion."
The spirit of compassion lies herein: the *Baiyi jiemmo* (Karmavācanā-śataika) clarifies five types of water filters (*parisrāvaṇa*).

First, the single-layered filter (*ekapārśva-parisrāvaṇa*) uses three or two feet of silk, made according to the size required by the occasion. Second, the two methods for the water jar (*ghaṭa*): the Yin-jar and the Yang-jar. Third, the *jun-chi*:
one strikes the mouth with silk and suspends it with a rope to sink into the water; when full, one draws it out. Fourth, the water-drawing filter (*pānīya-parisrāvaṇa*).
The *pañcakaṭhina* cloth is made of fine silk, measuring one *vyāma* square; it is used for filtering water by tying it over the mouth of a flask or placing it inside a bowl.
The mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*).
In Sanskrit, *khakkhara* means "staff with a clanging sound," so called because it produces a *khak-khak* sound when shaken; thus, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* calls it the "Sound Staff.
The *Khakkhara-sūtra* states that the Buddha told the bhikṣus: "You should receive and maintain the khakkhara. Why?
Because all Buddhas of the past, future, and present have held it. It is also called the "Staff of Wisdom" (*jñāna-daṇḍa*) and the "Staff of Virtue" (*guṇa-daṇḍa*).
Because it manifests the merit of wise conduct, it is the banner of the sages, the clear record of the worthy, and the standard of the Dharma.
Relying upon this staff, one eliminates afflictions and emerges from the three realms. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-ksudraka-vastu* states:

A bhikṣu entered deeply into the house of a lay elder while begging for food and consequently incurred censure and slander. The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "One may make a sound [while entering]."

Becoming aware of this, he immediately made "ha-ha" sounds, causing a clamor and inviting ridicule and reproach. The Buddha established a rule prohibiting this; consequently, he struck the gatekeeper with his fist.
The gatekeeper asked in astonishment, "Why have you broken down my door? He remained silent and offered no reply. The Buddha said, "One should make a *khakkhara* (monk’s staff).

The bhikṣus did not understand the Buddha's words regarding the staff. [The Buddha explained: "A ring should be attached to the head of the staff, circular like the rim of a cup (*zàn*), and a small [ring] should be fixed upon it."
The rings on the staff shake and produce sound to serve as a warning; when one has moved for a distance of one or two paces and no one hears it, one must immediately proceed further.
The *Wu-bai wen* (Five Hundred Questions) states that carrying the *khakkhara* (staff) has many purposes, such as being able to warn off evil insects, venomous creatures, and wild beasts.
Yi Jing (Yijing) states that the *khakkhara* consists of three parts: the upper part is of tin (*śrīkhaṇḍa*), while the middle is wood and the lower part is either ivory or horn. If there are two...
The six-pronged [vajra] with six rings was fashioned by Kāśyapa Buddha; the four-pronged [vajra] with twelve rings was fashioned by Śākyamuni Buddha.

This sutra further states that there are those with staffs that are identical, though their applications may differ—some having two prongs and some having four prongs, while the number of rings remains the same.
However, today I employ the teaching of the four-pronged [vajra] with twelve rings; as for the four prongs, they are used for this purpose.

The twelve rings, which sever the four modes of birth and contemplate the Four Noble Truths, represent the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination for the sake of unimpeded penetration.

The two prongs were established by the Tathāgata Kāśyapa to cause all sentient beings to keep in mind the two truths—the conventional truth and the ultimate truth—thereby establishing their meaning. Master Qi Chou was at Wangwu in Huai Prefecture.
When Shan heard of two tigers fighting, he resolved the conflict with his *khakkhara* (monk’s staff) and composed a verse, saying: "Originally I sought no fame, yet fame has come to seek me;
before the crag I resolved the strife of the two tigers, thereby obstructing the third fruit. Furthermore, Deng Yinfeng flew his staff through the air to resolve the conflict between two armies.
Because such are its superior merits, it should be upheld and maintained.

"Rosary" is the Sanskrit term *akṣamālā*, which in the Liang dynasty was translated as "counting-beads. It refers to an instrument for guiding those of inferior faculties to engage in recitation and cultivate their practice.
The *Bodhi-jambu-phala Sūtra* states: "In the past, there was a king named Vimalaprabha who addressed the Buddha, saying: 'My country is small and remote.'"

"Year after year, there have been bandits, epidemics, and high grain prices, leaving the people in distress. I am constantly uneasy; though the Dharma-treasury is profound and vast, I am unable to practice it in its entirety.

I only pray that you will graciously show me the essential points of the Dharma. The Buddha said, "Great King, if you wish to extinguish the afflictions, you should string together one hundred and eight wood *naga* seeds and always carry them with you. With a sincere mind, recite: 'Namo Buddhāya, Namo Dharmāya, [Namo Saṃghāya].'"
If one recites this even once more than a hundred times, it is as if there were no longer any distinction between oneself and the Saṃgha;

by proceeding gradually in this manner until ten million recitations are completed, reaching up to two hundred thousand times, with body and mind undisturbed, free from flattery and crookedness, at the end of life one will attain rebirth in the Yāma Heaven.

If one completes one million recitations, one shall eliminate the karmic fetters of the hundred-and-eight afflictions and obtain the fruit of eternal bliss. The King said: "I shall respectfully practice this, Mañjuśrī."
The *Sūtra on the Comparative Merit of Rosaries* states that the substances of rosaries vary;

when compared, reciting them once with a *huangzi* (Elaeocarpus) bead yields a thousandfold merit, with a lotus seed bead yields ten-thousandfold merit, and with a *bodhi* (Elaeocarpus) bead, the merit obtained is immeasurable.
Furthermore, in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Gavāmpati suffered from the ailment of "ox-chewing" (eructation), and the Buddha provided him with a rosary to prevent slander.
The rosary causes one to practice mindfulness of the Buddha; this is called the Dharma-gate of Single-Flavored Purity.

Even the accomplishment of the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha, rebirth in the Pure Land, and the realization of the patience of non-arising are all due to the immeasurable merit of the rosary (the one hundred and eight beads severing the one hundred and eight afflictions).
Regarding the sevenfold prostration to the Buddha, the *Mahāvaipulya Ratnakaraṇḍa Sūtra* states: The śrāvaka Jñānapradīpa asked Mañjuśrī, "How does one pay homage to the Buddha?
Mañjuśrī replied, "If one perceives the purity of the Dharma, this is called perceiving the purity of the Buddha. Whether body or mind, one is neither bowed nor raised, but remains upright."
Abiding thus, one is unmoving and unwavering; with a tranquil mind, one practices tranquil conduct—this is called paying homage to the Buddha-Dharma Garden.

[This concludes] the *Qi Zhong Li Fa* (The Sevenfold Methods of Paying Homage), translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Ratnamati. 1. **Homage of Pride**: This refers to performing the ritual according to one's rank and position while lacking a heart of reverence;
the mind wanders toward external objects, the five limbs are not fully prostrated, and the movement is like that of a pestle rising and falling. It is performed twice.

First is the prostration of coarse and formal deportment: when one sees a person, the body moves with haste to perform the greeting, and once the person has left, the body collapses and the mind grows weary;
this is because the mind is distracted while the mouth chants. Second is the prostration of physical and mental reverence:

upon hearing the name of the Buddha chanted, one immediately brings the Buddha to mind, and both body and mind become reverent, free from any sense of weariness or indolence. Third is the prostration that gives rise to pure wisdom.
"Ritual" (*li*) means to reach the Buddha’s realm and manifest according to the measure of one's own mind. To pay homage to one Buddha is to pay homage to all Buddhas;

to perform a single prostration is to pay homage to the entire Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), because the Buddha’s Dharma-body is all-pervasive and interfused. "Fivefold universal entry into the Dharma-realm" refers to ritual:

observing for oneself that the body, mind, and other phenomena have from the very beginning not been separate from the Dharma-realm, such that the Buddha and the self are equal. Now, I pay homage to this one [Buddha].

The Buddha then universally pays homage to all Buddhas of the Dharma-realm through the six correct contemplations of homage. This means that one pays homage to one's own Buddha without taking other Buddhas as an object. Why is this?
Because all sentient beings possess their own Buddha-nature, which is the equal and perfect enlightenment. Seventh is the homage of the equality of the true mark (*dharmatā*).
This means that previously there was still the act of homage and the contemplation of self and other as two distinct entities; now, in this single homage, there is neither self nor other.

Because the ordinary and the sage are of one essence and substance and function are non-dual, Mañjuśrī said: "The nature of the one who prostrates and the object of prostration is empty and quiescent.

The first three [verses] concern phenomena (*dharma*), while the latter four pertain to principle (*li*). Prostrating to the Buddha is thus; prostrating to a stūpa is likewise. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"When prostrating to the Buddha, one must not be like a mute sheep. Furthermore, when prostrating to a Buddha-stūpa, one should circumambulate to the right, just as the sun, moon, and stars revolve around Mount Sumeru.

There are five matters regarding the circumambulation of a mountain by turning to the left: (1) keep the head bowed and gaze at the ground; (2) do not tread upon insects; (3) do not look to the left or right;

(4) do not sleep on the ground; (5) do not converse with others. Furthermore, there are five blessings obtained from circumambulation: (1) in future lives one will obtain an upright and handsome appearance; (2) one will obtain a beautiful voice; (3) one will be reborn in the heavens; (4) one will be born as a king or noble; (5) one will attain the path of Nirvāṇa.

A Bodhisattva has three names: first, Mahāsattva (Great Being), referring to sentient beings with the mind of the Great Way; second, Vikrānta (Valiant One), referring to those who open the faith and confidence of sentient beings;
third, Mahāpuruṣa (Noble Person), referring to those who transcend ordinary people and the Lesser Vehicle.
The Bodhisattva’s three greatnesses are: first, the greatness of the vow; second, the greatness of practice;

and third, the greatness of benefiting sentient beings. Regarding the maintenance of precepts, there are three mentalities: first, the mentality of revulsion toward conditioned phenomena; second, the mentality of seeking to proceed toward enlightenment; and third, the mentality of compassion for sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are three pleasures: first, fame; second, gain and offerings; and third, being reborn in the heavens after death.
The Mahābhikṣu has three meanings: first, he destroys evil by cultivating precepts, concentration, and wisdom, thereby breaking through the delusions of views and thoughts;

second, he terrifies Māra, causing the Lord of Demons to fear his emergence from the triple world and feel dread; third, he is a mendicant who sustains the physical body and nourishes the life of wisdom, benefiting those who practice dāna.
The three types of *karmavācanā* are: first, the procedure with one person present; second, the procedure by mental recollection; and third, the procedure for the assembly.
The three robes sever the three poisons: the five-strip robe severs greed of the body, the seven-strip robe severs anger of the mouth, and the great robe (saṃghāṭī) severs delusion of the mind.
In the first division of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the Bhikṣu-prātimokṣa is expounded; in the second division, the Bhikṣuṇī-prātimokṣa along with the Upasampadā-khandhaka;
in the third division, the Varṣā-khandhaka; and in the fourth division, the Śayanāsana-khandhaka.

A bhikṣu possesses four dharmas: first, to confess and repent of one's transgressions six times during the day and night; second, to constantly mindfully recollect the Buddha and not deceive sentient beings;
third, to cultivate harmony and a respectful heart, free from anger and arrogance; fourth, to fully practice the six recollections as if extinguishing a fire on one's head.
The four dharmas of *karma* are: first, the dharma; second, the matter; third, the person; and fourth, the realm.
The four root afflictions are: first, greed; second, anger; third, delusion; and fourth, pride. The four dharmas for cultivation are:
first, to rather lose one's body and life than abandon the bodhicitta; second, to draw near to virtuous friends.
Third, not abandoning patience; fourth, relying on a place of tranquility.

Regarding the four categories of upāsakas: one who accepts all parts receives the three refuges and all the precepts; one who accepts a small part receives either one precept or two, three, or four precepts;
and one who accepts the full part completely receives the five precepts.

Regarding the category of precepts, the places of rebirth resulting from them differ: those who break the precepts are reborn among the three lower realms of animals, hungry ghosts, and hell-dwellers;

those who maintain the precepts are reborn among humans; those who maintain the precepts while also practicing the four dhyānas and the four formless absorptions (ārūpya-samādhi) are reborn above the six heavens of the desire realm;
those who maintain the precepts below that level attain the stage of Arhat; those in the middle attain the stage of Pratyekabuddha; and those at the highest level attain the path of Buddhahood.

A disciple observes the preceptor with four states of mind: first, as a close friend and teacher; second, as a teacher to be revered and obeyed; third, as a teacher from whom one fears transgression; and fourth, as a teacher to be honored.

There are four kinds of profound kindness: first, that of the father; second, that of the mother, for they give birth to one’s body and thus must be repaid; and third, that of the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata.
Regarding the Dharma-preacher:
the Buddha should manifest birth in Kapilavastu, attain enlightenment in Magadha, preach the Dharma in Vārāṇasī, and enter parinirvāṇa in the city of Kuśinagara. These are the four places.
There are four kinds of śramaṇas: first, the śramaṇa of mere deportment, called a bhikṣu in name only; second, the śramaṇa of outward appearance and dress, called a bhikṣu like a banner;
third, the śramaṇa of reputation, called a deceitful bhikṣu; and fourth, the śramaṇa of actual practice, called a bhikṣu who acts according to the Dharma.
Of these, the first three are not true śramaṇas yet claim to be so; only the last one is a true śramaṇa.
The Gate is a true śramaṇa. There are four times for eating:
at dawn, the food of the devas; at midday, the food of the Buddhas of the three ages; in the afternoon, the food of animals;
and at dusk, the food of ghosts and spirits.

There are four benefits for requiring food: to provide sustenance for the body so that it may cultivate the Path; to nourish the parasites within the body; to bestow merit upon the donor; and to destroy the hunger of those who follow external paths. There are four intentions behind begging for food:
first, to benefit all sentient beings; second, to subdue arrogance; third, to realize that the body is subject to suffering; [and fourth, to maintain the purity of livelihood].
Fourth, regarding the removal of obstructions:
the Vinaya has four meanings. First, it is the level ground within the Buddha-dharma, from which all myriad virtues arise.
Second, all sons of the Buddha rely upon the precepts to abide, and all sentient beings depend upon the precepts for their existence. Third, it is the path to... [the text continues].
The fourth is the initial gateway to *nirvāṇa* and the jeweled ornament of the Buddha-dharma, for it is able to adorn the Buddha-dharma.

By practicing humility, one attains four kinds of merit: first, one remains far removed from the evil realms and does not undergo rebirth as an animal; second, one is not subjected to contempt or disparagement;
third, one is constantly revered by humans and devas; and fourth, wicked friends, enemies, and adversaries cannot assail or overcome one.
A bodhisattva practices four dharmas: first, skillfully discerning that which is manifested from one's own mind; second, contemplating that external natures lack intrinsic existence;
third, abandoning views of arising, abiding, and ceasing; and fourth, attaining the excellent joy of the noble wisdom of self-realization.

Of the alms-food obtained, one should offer one-fourth to fellow practitioners of the holy life, a second portion to the destitute and beggars, a third to various spirits and deities, and keep the fourth portion for oneself.

A bhikṣu should not frequent five places: first, the residence of a government official; second, a tavern; third, the house of a butcher; fourth, the quarters of a prostitute; [and fifth, a royal palace].
The five *caṇḍāla* dwellings of the householders;
the five things for which a bhikṣu need not attend an invitation: first, dwelling in tranquility; second, the preaching of the Dharma by devas;
third, observing the sick; fourth, guarding bedding and requisites; fifth, the training rules established by the precepts.

There are five factors that assist the precepts: first, faith; second, self-respect (*hrī*); third, shame before others (*apatrāpya*); fourth, virtuous friends; and fifth, revering the precepts. There are five degenerations resulting from breaking the precepts:
first, seeking wealth but not obtaining it; second, even if obtained, it is dissipated; third, the assembly does not accept one's respect;
fourth, an evil reputation spreads; and fifth, after death, one enters hell.

The five benefits of the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*) are: first, supreme peace and security; second, the non-distraction of the mind; third, the fear of Māra; fourth, distinguishing oneself from non-Buddhists;
and fifth, the ease with which the mind is stilled.
The five virtues of a *bhikṣu* are likened to those of a renunciant: first, his physical nature is supple, which is likened to the ability to subdue body and speech.
1. The metaphor of spreading branches and vines in all directions illustrates the broad application of the Dharma to guide others in an unceasing succession; 2.

The metaphor of fragrance wafting far illustrates how the perfume of one's precepts and virtue is renowned among the multitude; 3. The metaphor of being able to cure pain illustrates the ability to sever the poisonous harm of the afflictions (*kleśa*);
4. The metaphor of not turning one’s back to the sun illustrates always facing the Buddha-sun.
When begging for alms, one should avoid five types of households: first, those that shout out their wares; second, those of the Caṇḍālas;
third, those that sell liquor; fourth, government offices;

and fifth, the houses of prostitutes. When entering a layperson’s house, there are five rules: first, speak softly upon entering the gate; second, restrain body, speech, and mind; third, humble one's posture; [fourth, ...]
He well guards his sense faculties and maintains the five modes of deportment with dignity, causing others to give rise to wholesome states.
For five reasons, the great bhikṣu exerts himself: first, to repay the Buddha’s kindness; second, to nurture the Buddha-dharma;
third, to eliminate the self-conceit of inferior and ordinary persons; and fourth, to subdue the arrogance of future disciples.
Fifth, because it initiates meritorious karma for the future; furthermore, according to the Vinaya, a bhikṣu is permitted to personally construct a vihāra.

Therein, five dharmas are required for confession: first, baring the right shoulder; second, placing the right knee on the ground; third, joining the palms with a sincere mind; fourth, prostrating with the head and face at the feet;
and fifth, declaring the name of one’s own offense.

The *Pañcavargika Vinaya* consists of: (1) the rules on the *pārājika* offenses; (2) the rules on the *pārājika* offenses for nuns; (3) the rules on receiving the precepts, robes, medicine, food, and so forth;
(4) the rules on the settlement of disputes; and (5) the miscellaneous rules on schisms in the Saṃgha and other matters.
The five kinds of repentance are: first, there is no need for repentance; one should constantly contemplate the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
Second, filially support one’s parents and show reverence to teachers and elders. Third, govern the state according to the True Dharma so that the people do not become deranged.
Fourth, on the six days of the fast (*ṣaḍ-upoṣadha*), issue commands throughout the realm to practice non-killing. Fifth, have deep faith in cause and effect and know that the Buddha does not perish.
A bhikṣu possesses five virtues: first, the terrifier of Māra; second, the seeker of alms; third, the one of pure precepts; fourth, the one of pure livelihood; and fifth, the destroyer of evil.
Regarding the five categories of offenses, there are four *pārājika* rules: for bhikṣus, four articles—killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying;
for bhikṣuṇīs, eight articles. There are thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules: thirteen for bhikṣus and seventeen for bhikṣuṇīs. There are thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* rules...
The ninety *śīlavarga* offenses for monks (*bhikṣu*), the ninety offenses for monks, the one hundred and seventy-eight offenses for nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*),
the four *pratideśanīya* offenses for monks, the eight *pratideśanīya* offenses for nuns, the one hundred *duṣkṛta* (or *āpatti*) offenses that must be studied,
the one hundred offenses for monks, the one hundred offenses for nuns, and the two hundred offenses for monks.
Regarding the fifty rules for nuns and the three hundred and forty-eight rules— of which there are now only forty-one—
it is because two *aniyata* (undetermined) rules and the seven methods for settling disputes (*saptadharmāḥ saṃghāvaśeṣa*) have been added, bringing the total back to fifty rules.

The five precepts lead to rebirth in the heavens: first, by abstaining from killing, one is born in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings; second, by abstaining from stealing, one is born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;

third, by abstaining from sexual misconduct, one is born in the Yāma Heaven; fourth, by abstaining from false speech, one is born in the Tuṣita Heaven; and fifth, by abstaining from intoxicants, one is born in the Nirmāṇarati and Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heavens.

There are five kinds of ācāryas: first, the teacher of renunciation, by whom one relies upon to obtain ordination; second, the karmavācanā teacher, who bestows the precepts and performs the ritual acts;
third, the instructor teacher, who teaches the scriptures and the rules of deportment; fourth, the sūtra-recitation teacher, from whom one receives the four-line verses and so forth of the sūtras;
and fifth, the upādhyāya, upon whom one relies to study the precepts for ten summer retreats before becoming a teacher to others.

There are five types of questions that should not be answered: questions asked for the sake of testing, questions asked because there is no doubt, questions asked so as not to cause remorse for what has been transgressed, questions asked for the sake of receiving [teachings], and questions asked for the sake of refutation.
Regarding the five dharmas of leaving the household life: first, one leaves home having resolved the mind and cherishes the Noble Path within; second, one alters one's physical appearance...
1. To don the dharma robes; 2. To utterly cast aside body and life to honor and revere the path of the Dharma; 3. To forever sever ties with kin and loved ones, being neither partial nor biased;
4. To aspire toward the Mahāyāna for the sake of delivering all sentient beings.
The five benefits of the *yānjī* (willow branch) are: first, it prevents the mouth from smelling foul; second, it prevents the mouth from becoming bitter;
third, it removes heat and can dispel wind; fourth, it eliminates wind and also removes heat; fifth, it aids digestion, removes phlegm and mucus, and clarifies the eyes.
Observing the five merits of the precepts results in a firm and excellent foundation for ethical discipline; one can decisively resolve disputes among the assembly without fear or regret;
one is capable of providing liberating explanations; and by properly maintaining the precepts, one causes the True Dharma to endure for a long time.

The Dharma for relying on a preceptor for five years: after five years, one must know five things—know the gravity of offenses, know the *karmavācanā* (formal procedures), know the *ācārya*, and [know the rules regarding] the five kinds of *kāṣāya*.
Those who enter my Dharma—even those who have committed grave offenses or hold wrong views—[attain liberation] in a single thought-moment.
Those who respect it with a reverent heart will surely receive predictions of enlightenment within the Three Vehicles;

devas, nāgas, and spirits who can honor even a small portion of this *kāṣāya* shall immediately attain non-retrogression in the Three Vehicles. If humans or spirits obtain a *kāṣāya*, even if it is only four inches in size, their food and drink will be sufficient.
If there are sentient beings who are at odds with one another, by recollecting the power of the *kāṣāya*, they will immediately become reconciled.
If one maintains even a small portion of this loving-kindness with reverence and respect, one will always surpass others;
even if a dragon wears but a single thread [of this merit], it shall be spared from the calamity of the garuḍa, and one shall avoid shedding the blood of a Buddha.

The five kinds of Triple Refuge counteract the heterodox; the Five Precepts, Eight Precepts, Ten Precepts, and Full Ordination correspond to the five punishments, the five elements, and the five categories of offenses: *pārājika* corresponds to death and earth; *saṃghāvaśeṣa* to flowing water;
*pāyattika* to exile; *pratideśanīya* to the rod; and *duṣkṛta* to flogging with wood.
The twenty-five guardian deities of the five precepts: 1. *Cāruvīyudhani* (Guardian of Not Killing) 2.
*Rundharisundhanī* 3. *Vilucanaśepa* 4. *Dharamadhi* 5.
*Sara-hvanīhavā* [Regarding] Not Stealing: 1. *Jimā-abhidhata* (Guardian of Not Stealing) 2. [Omitted]

Now, through self-awakening, one may preserve steadfast integrity; meeting any path, one remains unobstructed, and as soon as a thought arises, one is alert. Unstained by the six sense objects, the three poisons are thereby purified.
Cease further beating the drum that causes turbidity, lest you lose your original luminosity; it is fitting to clarify yourself from within, so that you may return to the primal essence.
The Great Master Qingliang Chengguan encouraged himself with ten matters:
his body did not cast off the outward appearance of a śramaṇa; his mind did not contravene the regulations of the Tathāgata; while seated, he did not turn his back on the sutras of the Dharma-realm;
his nature was unstained by the objects of emotional obstruction; his feet did not tread upon the dust of a bhikṣuṇī’s convent; and his side did not touch that of a layperson.
His eyes did not look upon colors that were not in accordance with propriety; his tongue did not taste delicacies served after noon; his hands never let go of the *cintāmaṇi* bead;
and he never stayed overnight apart from his robes and bowl.
Compiled by the Bhikṣu Longrui of Huangbo Mountain in the first month of summer in the Guiyou year of the Chongzhen era.
